Compared sample by sample at 44.1k and 48k to 705.6k and 768k, from 176.4k and 192k sources, and on two music tracks; not compared from 88.2k, where the members' readings agree, nor at any output rate other than 705.6k and 768k. In the one conversion across rate families the atlas tried, HQPlayer refused both. Beyond the dataset, in a test on engine 6.2.4, HQPlayer refused closed-form, sinc-medium and poly-sinc-ext2-short, described with “up” as sinc-M is, in every downward conversion tried: read plainly, filters described with “up” are made for upsampling, not for decimation. In that test HQPlayer converted 352.8k to 176.4k with sinc-M and refused it in none of the test's conversions; sinc-Mx was not tried.

pairs.note: Fixed against adaptive seventh order: less noise in band with the adaptive one, and a two-tone that stays stable to 0 dBFS at more rates.
The same ext2 poly-sinc, with and without apodizing: with apodizing, the cutoff moves further below the source's Nyquist, the length barely changes.
The same Gaussian poly-sinc, with and without apodizing: with apodizing, the cutoff moves further below the source's Nyquist, the length barely changes.
The same Gaussian sinc, without and with apodizing: with apodizing, the cutoff moves further below the source's Nyquist, the length barely changes.
Without and with extended compensation, one generation apart: more noise in band with EC, and slower on the measuring host.
The seventh-order EC modulator, Gen6 against Gen7: more noise in band with Gen7.
The ext2 and Gaussian windows at one cutoff, as the author pairs them: a steeper transition with longer ringing, or a wider one with shorter ringing.
Two Gaussian lengths: a wider transition, shorter ringing and a roll-off that starts a little lower, or a narrower transition with longer ringing.
One apodizing Gaussian design at two lengths: a much wider transition with much shorter ringing, or a narrow one with long ringing.
Two sinc lengths with the cutoff on the source's Nyquist: a wide transition with short ringing, or a narrow one with long ringing.
One-bit against pseudo-multi-bit, both seventh-order EC tuned for DSD512 and above, three generations apart: far more noise in band with the pseudo-multi-bit.
Fifth against seventh order, both Gen7 EC: more noise in and just above the audio band with the fifth.
Fifth against seventh order without EC, both Gen3: more noise in band with the fifth.
Linear against minimum phase on one apodizing hi-res magnitude: ringing on both sides of a transient, or only after it.
Linear against intermediate phase on one magnitude: symmetric ringing, or less of it before a transient and more after.
Linear against minimum phase on one magnitude: ringing on both sides of a transient, or only after it, with 20 kHz arriving later.
The same Gen7 modulator, without and with the tuning for DSD512 and above: with the tuned one, far less noise in band from DSD256 up.
The fixed seventh order, without and with the tuning for DSD256 and above: with the tuned one, far less noise in band and a two-tone that stays stable to 0 dBFS.

sources.quote: The apodizing filters in HQPlayer are designed to correct the problems from these filters.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Why do audiophiles like HQ Player?” #48

sources.quote: These errors are from recording ADC digital filter, or from production chain software tools.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2015-2023]” #1720
Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2023]” #61

sources.quote: poly-sinc-ext3 is for poly-sinc-ext2, what poly-sinc-gauss-xla is for poly-sinc-gauss-long.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2023]” #480
Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Further information on 5.11 [EC Modulators and AHM]” #2

sources.quote: It uses different noise shaping curve to provide more headroom in 100 kHz band by trading some music bandwidth (from 200 kHz at DSD512 to 100 kHz), it can afford this since the bandwidth doubles at every doubling of sampling rate.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Further information on 5.11 [EC Modulators and AHM]” #10

sources.quote: Hence also being the current default on new HQPlayer installations.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Further information on 5.11 [EC Modulators and AHM]” #10

sources.quote: It was renamed to poly-sinc-ext2-xla to align naming with the poly-sinc-gauss group. … ext2 and gauss are now offered in matching pairs with matching parameters.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2024]” #1165

sources.quote: From objective perspective all the -ul/-ligh/-fast/-super are very good. Each has a slightly different sonic character though, so worth trying to see which one you prefer.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “HQPlayer Desktop thread” #2099

sources.quote: Recommended is DSD512 output or higher, but it is allowed for DSD256 (although not recommended). It is not allowed for lower output rates though.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2024]” #1362

sources.quote: sinc-M is practically a fixed length (million tap) version of poly-sinc-ext2-xla. While sinc-S and sinc-Mx are varying length version, where the number of taps changes as function of conversion ratio, so that it has same length in time regardless of the ratio (million taps at 16x factor), hence also steepness is always the same regardless of factor.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “DAC Corrections” #159

sources.quote: Gauss is particularly correct on transients, while keeping very good correctness also on the harmonic constructs. While ext2 is specifically focusing on harmonic constructs. Then xtr is more like "best of traditional filter approach", without any specific focus otherwise.
sources.where: Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2024]” #1440
Roon › Audio Gear Talk › HQ Player › “Which HQP Filter are you using? [2024]” #1447

sources.quote: In PCM mode, each filter in both slots, the output rate fixed and the adaptive output rate off, HQPlayer converted a DSD64 track to 176.4k before the filter. closed-form, sinc-medium and poly-sinc-ext2-short, described with “up”, played 1:1 at 44.1k, 88.2k and 352.8k and upward from 44.1k to 88.2k and from the DSD64 track to 352.8k, and HQPlayer refused them in every downward conversion tried: 88.2k to 44.1k, 352.8k to 176.4k, and the DSD64 track to 88.2k. sinc-M, described with “up” too, converted 352.8k to 176.4k, and HQPlayer refused it in no conversion tried. FFT and FIR, described without “up”, were refused at 1:1 and played every downward conversion tried; poly-sinc-ext2, without “up” too, played every conversion tried.
